stances.claim: The Makabayan bloc in the House has again filed bills to revise the party-list law (RA 7941) to 'ensure that it stays true to its original purpose of serving the marginalized' and underrepresented; Sen. Hontiveros filed a similar Senate bill targeting the dynasties.

The original sin is imbedded not only in the law but also in its creator, the 1987 Constitution, which experimentally instituted the party-list system it borrowed from parliamentary systems and tried to integrate it into our presidential system.

While the experiment was well-intended, it was flawed -- the presidential system is meant to be partnered with proportional representation in the House and by the autonomous equality of the component states, as in the United States. For decades, we adopted the US presidential system from US enactments (Jones Law + Tydings-McDuffie Act) that happily blended with our culture of patriarchal and matriarchal supremacy.
stances.rhetorical_move: well-intended-but-flawed + US-presidential-history Jones/Tydings-McDuffie citation + cultural-patriarchal/matriarchal blending

stances.claim: To be accurate, the 1987 framers provided not just for proportional representation in the House but also for party-list-elected representatives constituting 20% of total membership, with one-half of those seats for three consecutive terms filled by 'labor, peasant, urban poor, indigenous cultural communities, women, youth, and such other sectors, as may be provided by law, except the religious sector.' In short, other than the 20% constitution and the three-term-half-marginalized rule, the Charter did not define what this political animal was, nor the timeline of the experiment.

Neither did Congress define the mongrel -- while it tried to fulfill its constitutional duty 'as provided by law,' it merely limited the party-list electoral winners to those who obtained at least 2% of the total votes cast for all party-list candidates; it did not define the nature of the mongrel.

In Veterans v. Comelec (Oct 6 2000), the SC upheld the 2% statutory restriction, ruling that the 20% constitutional limit was merely directory, not mandatory; thereafter in Bagong Bayani v. Comelec (June 26 2001), it held that only the parties and organizations and their nominees who belong to the marginalized and underrepresented were deemed qualified. These two early decisions CJP wrote for the Court pointed to the textual ambiguities and asked Congress to enact new legislation to define and clarify the mongrel -- while awaiting congressional action, the Court limited via the two decisions the party-list winners to only a few seats (about 15).
stances.rhetorical_move: Veterans-and-Bagong-Bayani CJP-authorship + textual-ambiguities-flagging + 15-seats limit historical anchor

stances.claim: After CJP retired, the Court in Banat v. Comelec (April 21 2009) voided the 2% bar of the party-list law, reasoning that the 20% could never be attained mathematically with that bar; and in Atong Paglaum v. Comelec (April 2 2013) ruled that party-list candidates and their nominees need not belong to the marginalized and underrepresented -- rather, it was open to all.
stances.rhetorical_move: post-retirement Banat + Atong-Paglaum + open-to-all reversal narration

stances.claim: As a result, the dynasties invaded the system, the veteran politicians misused it to circumvent the three-term constitutional limit, the rich owned it as an easy election tool, and the powerful misrepresented the lowly and weak in Congress; moreover, the House had to increase its budget by 20% more to fund the party-list solons, aside from also increasing the pork barrel and flood control insertions.
stances.rhetorical_move: four-fold invasion cascade (dynasties + veterans + rich + powerful) + 20%-budget-increase + pork-and-flood-control consequence

stances.claim: Given that the House at present is composed of 20% party-list solons, CJP doubts whether the proposed reforms and refinements eliminating dynasties and power blocs would succeed -- in his humble view, only a Con-con (not a constituent assembly) can abolish the mongrel or limit its membership only to the marginalized and underrepresented.

In writing those two early decisions, CJP exposed his rather activist streak -- interpreting liberally to attain the avowed aim of serving the marginalized and underrepresented; he was guided by the spirit rather than by the wording of the laws. On the other hand, his successors interpreted the Constitution verba legis or according to its text -- they ruled that 'shall' was mandatory (meaning 20% must always be party-list) and that the 20% could not be attained if winners were limited to (1) those who garnered at least 2% and (2) marginalized-and-underrepresented; so they opened the gates, and the flood rushed in.
stances.rhetorical_move: activist-streak self-disclosure + spirit-over-wording vs verba-legis interpretive-school contrast + opened-the-gates closing metaphor

one_paragraph_summary: Anchored on the Makabayan bloc's renewed party-list-revision bills + Hontiveros's parallel Senate bill targeting dynasties, CJP diagnoses the system's 'original sin' -- the 1987 Constitution experimentally grafted a parliamentary party-list mechanism onto an inherited US presidential system meant to partner with proportional representation and component-state autonomy (per Jones Law and Tydings-McDuffie Act). The Charter set a 20% party-list House ceiling and a three-term half-marginalized rule, but never defined the mongrel; Congress added only a 2% statutory threshold. CJP's own pre-retirement authorship of Veterans v. Comelec (Oct 6 2000, upholding the 2% threshold and ruling the 20% directory) and Bagong Bayani v. Comelec (June 26 2001, limiting qualified parties to marginalized-and-underrepresented) limited the early party-list winners to about 15 seats. After his retirement, Banat (April 21 2009) voided the 2% bar and Atong Paglaum (April 2 2013) opened the system to all, after which dynasties + veteran politicians + the rich + the powerful invaded -- driving a 20% House budget increase plus pork-barrel and flood-control insertions. He confesses his earlier activist 'spirit-of-the-law' streak versus his successors' verba-legis school, and concludes that only a Con-con (not a Con-Ass) can abolish or relimit the mongrel.
